options: Every function needs an explicit lifetime
Each elided input reference gets its own distinct lifetime
All references share one lifetime by default
Only the first argument gets a lifetime
quiz.explain: Rule 1: every elided (unwritten) lifetime among the input references is treated as its own distinct lifetime parameter.

quiz.q: Under elision rule 2, when is the single input lifetime assigned to the output?
options: Never automatically
When there's exactly one input lifetime
When there are exactly two input lifetimes
Only for methods
quiz.explain: Rule 2: if there is exactly one input lifetime (elided or explicit), it's assigned to every elided output lifetime.

quiz.q: Under elision rule 3, whose lifetime is assigned to elided outputs?
options: The first parameter's, always
&self's (or &mut self's) lifetime, when the function is a method
The return type's own lifetime
There is no rule 3
quiz.explain: Rule 3: if one of the inputs is &self or &mut self, that lifetime is assigned to all elided output lifetimes — this is why most getter methods need no annotation.

quiz.q: Why does `fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str` need an explicit lifetime?
options: It doesn't — elision would infer it automatically
There are two input lifetimes and no &self, so neither rule 2 nor rule 3 applies
Only functions named 'longest' need lifetimes
String slices always require explicit lifetimes
quiz.explain: With two distinct input references and no &self parameter, none of the three elision rules produce a unique answer, so the compiler requires an explicit annotation.

quiz.q: Why does `struct Excerpt { text: &str }` fail to compile?
options: Structs can't hold references at all
A struct holding a reference needs a lifetime parameter so the compiler knows how long the struct itself can live
str must always be owned, not borrowed
Only tuple structs can hold references
quiz.explain: The compiler needs a named lifetime parameter (e.g. Excerpt<'a>) to tie the struct's own validity to the reference it stores.

quiz.q: Why does a string literal like "hello" have type &'static str?
options: Because all strings default to 'static
Because it's embedded directly in the compiled binary and is never freed during the program's run
Because the compiler heap-allocates it once at startup
It doesn't — string literals have no lifetime
quiz.explain: String literals are baked into the binary at compile time, so they're valid for the entire run of the program — hence 'static.

quiz.q: What does a `T: 'static` trait bound actually require?
options: That every value of T is a compile-time constant
That T contains no references with a lifetime shorter than 'static — i.e. it owns its data or only borrows 'static data
That T must be declared at the top level of the program
That T implements Copy
quiz.explain: T: 'static means T doesn't contain any non-'static borrows; an ordinary owned value like a local String satisfies it trivially, even though the variable itself is short-lived.

quiz.q: In `fn print_it<T: Debug + 'static>(value: T)`, why does passing an owned `String` compile fine even though the variable is a short-lived local?
options: It doesn't compile — Strings can never satisfy 'static
The String owns its data outright, so it has no borrows that could expire early, satisfying 'static regardless of the variable's own scope
The String is secretly treated as a string literal
'static only applies to references, never to this kind of bound
quiz.explain: 'static as a bound is about what a type borrows, not how long the variable lives — an owned String has nothing to expire, so it satisfies T: 'static.

quiz.q: Why is reaching for `'static` to fix a lifetime error usually the wrong move?
options: It's literally impossible to compile
It usually just relocates the bug — now a borrowed value can't be passed in at all where 'static is required
'static bounds were removed in newer Rust editions
It always makes the program slower at runtime
quiz.explain: Forcing a 'static bound doesn't fix the underlying ownership issue; it often just makes it impossible to pass in the borrowed value you actually had, pushing you toward cloning or restructuring ownership instead.

flashcards.back: Each elided input reference gets its own distinct lifetime parameter.
If there's exactly one input lifetime, it's assigned to every elided output lifetime.
If one input is &self/&mut self, its lifetime is assigned to every elided output lifetime.

flashcards.front: When do you need to write an explicit lifetime by hand?
flashcards.back: When none of the three elision rules produce a single answer — typically two or more distinct input references with no &self.

flashcards.front: Why does a struct holding a reference need a lifetime parameter?
flashcards.back: So the compiler can tie the struct's own validity to the lifetime of the data it borrows, preventing the struct from outliving that data.
They're embedded directly in the compiled binary, so they're valid for the entire program run.

flashcards.front: What does a `T: 'static` bound actually mean?
flashcards.back: T contains no references shorter-lived than 'static — it either owns its data or only borrows 'static data. It does not mean the value itself is global.

flashcards.front: Does an ordinary local `String` satisfy a `T: 'static` bound?
flashcards.back: Yes — it owns its data outright, so it has nothing to expire early, even though the variable itself has a normal, short scope.
